column2: The Grey Stranger

The storm came out of a clear sky and it did not behave like weather. It hunted the fleet ship by ship, and when it was done there was only your hull on the reef, burning, and the sea full of drowned men.

In the wreck of your cabin, with the water at his ankles, a grey stranger sits at your own chessboard. He has set up the pieces. He does not look at the storm.

"Play me," he says, "and I give you time. Every move you make out there is a move here. Refuse, and I will only watch."

The storm came out of a clear sky with a grudge in it. It broke the fleet ship by ship and left your hull on the reef with the hold full of sea.\n\nOn the last dry plank sits a grey stranger with a board of carved stone, every piece a king of the Karaks. "Gazul's hall is far," he says, "and you have not earned your seat in it yet. Play me, dawi. Every deed you do out there is a move here. Refuse, and I will only keep the tally."

The storm had a voice, and it was singing. It took the fleet ship by ship and left your hull on the reef, the sea full of the dead.\n\nIn the wreck of your cabin a grey stranger sits at a board of white and black jade, as patient as the mountains. "Your people count their lives in centuries," he says, "and still they end. Play me, and I give you a few more. Every choice you make out there is a move here. Refuse, and I will only watch."

They gave you a pistol with one shot in it, a bottle with one mouthful, and a sandbar that the tide will cover by nightfall. Your own flag dwindled on the horizon with the mate at the wheel.

When the light goes, there is a grey stranger sitting on the sand beside you with a chessboard on his knees. The water does not wet him.

"Play me," he says, "and I give you time. Refuse, and I will only watch."
Set up the pieces.
I do not play with you.
The game with Death begins. Every act of your story is one move. Good moves now buy a longer life at the end.
Death will only watch. The best your story can end in is a draw.
Somewhere, Death frowns and moves a piece back. (A good move in your game.)
Somewhere, Death smiles and takes a piece. (A bad move in your game.)

Too long at sea, too little gold, and a captain who will get us all killed for a legend. The mate says it to the whole crew, and the crew does not argue.\n\nThey take the flagship. They take your sword and your coat. The mate will sail home with a sad story of how you were washed overboard in a storm, and your heir will thank him for it.
Curse his name to the deep.

You wake on black shingle with gulls arguing over you. A grey skerry in the Sea of Claws, rocks, heather and a long-house with its roof fallen in. Far to the south, they have already held your funeral. Your heir sat in your chair at the feast and nobody told them to get up.

You wake in cold surf with the mist so thick you cannot see your own hands. An island off Albion, where the stones stand in rings and something walks the fens at night. At home there was a funeral without a body. Your heir rules now.
You wake on white sand under a sun like a hammer. A southern island, palms, a ruined watchtower and a spring of brackish water. At home they wept, read your will and gave everything to your heir.

You wake in warm shallows with something large moving under the water nearby. A Lustrian key, jungle to the waterline, and the stone of an older people under the roots. At home you are a name on a tomb. Your heir rules now.

You wake on pale sand in sight of Ulthuan's mountains, and no ship will come near. One of the outer isles, where the Asur lay their old wars to rest. At home they sang your lament and gave your seat to your heir.
Alive. Still alive.
Your titles at home have gone to your heir as if you had died. You hold this island now, and nothing else.

At low tide the wreck shows on the reef, ribs and all. There are casks in the hold, tools, powder, coin, and the sea will take all of it at the next storm.\n\nOr you could stay on the headland and keep a great fire burning, so that any passing ship knows a lord is here.
Swim out to the wreck.
Keep the beacon burning.

You cut a notch in a post for every day. There are a great many notches now.\n\nThe island will feed you, if you let it. You could build properly, a stockade, a shelter, a garden. Or you could live as the beasts do, off the hunt.
Build a stockade.
Live off the hunt.

There is a bare footprint on the beach, and it is not yours. You follow it to a fire, and at the fire is [castaway_companion.GetFirstName], a Norscan thrown up here by another storm, as thin as you and twice as wary.

There is a bare footprint on the beach, and it is not yours. It leads into the mist and to [castaway_companion.GetFirstName], an islander of Albion with tattooed arms and a spear, who has been watching you for a month.
There is a bare footprint on the beach, and it is not yours. It leads you to [castaway_companion.GetFirstName], a Southlander fisher who was left here to die by slavers and did not.
There is a bare footprint on the beach, and it is not yours. It leads to [castaway_companion.GetFirstName], an Amazon of Lustria, who has a blowpipe at your throat before you see her.
There is a bare footprint on the beach, and it is not yours. It leads to [castaway_companion.GetFirstName], an old Asur who came to the isle to die in peace and is very put out to find company.
A friend, at last.
You will serve me.

On the far side of the island there is a cell of stone, books stacked to the ceiling, and a sorcerer, [castaway_magister.GetFirstName], exiled from his own land with his daughter [castaway_daughter.GetFirstName]. In a split pine behind the cell an air spirit is bound, singing to itself. In chains by the door crouches the misshapen son of the witch who ruled the island before the sorcerer came.\n\n"I am sorry about your ships," [castaway_magister.GetFirstName] says. "I needed one to come to my shore. I raised the storm."
Then you owe me. Teach me.
Split the pine and free the spirit.
Strike off the witch's son's chains.

[castaway_magister.GetFirstName] has watched you for a season. "My daughter will not grow old on this rock," he says. "Take her into your house. One of your sons, or the friend the sea gave you. Or let her choose for herself."
To my son.
To [castaway_companion.GetFirstName].
She chooses for herself.

The chains fall off and the witch's son, [castaway_witchson.GetFirstName], stands up for the first time in years. Behind him the whole island stands up with him. In the cell [castaway_magister.GetFirstName] reaches for his staff, and the sky goes dark.
Down with the sorcerer!

The old hall above the landing has a curse on it. Every night something comes up out of the bog behind it, grey and stinking and as tall as the roof, and drags off whoever sleeps nearest the door. The islanders call it the troll. They say it hates the sound of laughter.

The old hall above the landing has a curse on it. Every night something comes out of the fen, one-eyed, scaled, dragging a tail, and takes whoever sleeps nearest the door. The islanders will not say its name, but they draw it in the mud with a single eye.
The old hall above the landing has a curse on it. Every night a ghul of the reefs climbs up out of the sea caves, wet, blind and starving, and takes whoever sleeps nearest the door.

The old hall above the landing has a curse on it. Every night a cold-blooded thing of the swamp comes up the beach, all teeth and scales, and takes whoever sleeps nearest the door. It is older than the hall. It is older than men.

The old hall above the landing has a curse on it. Every night a mist-wight of the old elf wars walks out of the barrow behind it and takes whoever sleeps nearest the door. It wears armour no smith has made in five thousand years.
I hold the hall myself.
Send [castaway_companion.GetFirstName].
Bar the doors and wait for dawn.

The thing is driven off, an arm torn away, and it crawled home to die. Now its mother has come for revenge, and she took two men from the hall last night.\n\nThe blood trail leads down to a black mere where nothing grows. The water is warm. Something old is waiting at the bottom, and there is a glint of a great sword down there, made for hands far bigger than yours.
Into the water.
[castaway_companion.GetFirstName] goes down instead.
Leave the mere alone.

The hall stands again, the roof new and the doors hung, and there is a fire in it every night now. The islanders come back to it with fish, ale and their own quarrels for you to judge. The few who lived through the wreck with you swear to you again on the new hearth.
Light the fires in the hall.

One morning there is a sail on the horizon, and it is coming in. A trader, lost, needing water. The captain stares at you as if you were a ghost, and then he says your name.\n\nHe can carry you home. Or he can carry a letter, and you can stay where you are.
Home!
I stay, as Lord of the Isle.
I stay. Send for my family.

A ship has come in with [From.GetTitledName] on board, a lord you buried years ago, thin, brown and very much alive. They want everything back: the seat, the titles, the chair at the head of the table.
Welcome home. It is all yours again.
The dead stay dead. This is an impostor.

[From.GetTitledName] will not open the gates. They have told the court you are an impostor, a pirate's trick, a drowned man's ghost. Some of your old retainers came out to the quay anyway, and looked at your face, and did not go back in.
The Return of the Drowned Lord!
Let them keep it.

The gates open. [From.GetTitledName] comes out to meet you, and after a long moment kneels. The old hall is the same and everyone in it is older. If the mate who stole your ship sat at this table, he sits in the dungeon now.
The island stays mine as well.
The island goes to [castaway_companion.GetFirstName].

There is a feast for your return, and at the high table sits [castaway_old_spouse.GetTitledName], who wore black for you and then stopped. There is someone new beside them. Your old bow still hangs on the wall. Nobody has been able to string it since you left.
String the old bow.
Let them be.
The Last Move

He is waiting at the end of your bed, the grey stranger, with the board between his knees. He looks at it a long time.\n\nThen he lays his king down on its side. "Well played," he says. "I will come back. Not soon."

He is waiting at the end of your bed, the grey stranger, with the board between his knees. Neither side can win from here, and you both know it.\n\n"Later," he says, and puts the pieces back in the box one by one. "Something is sleeping under your island. When it wakes, I will be there."

He is waiting at the end of your bed, the grey stranger, with the board between his knees. He moves one piece.\n\n"Checkmate," he says, not unkindly. "I will not take you today. But I have taken the years you were saving."
Death tips over his king.
Later, then.
Checkmate.
Years from now, in your old age, something will wake under the island.

You are old now. Last night a thief went into the barrow under the hill and stole a cup, and this morning the hall is burning. Something is coiled over the island with wings that blot out the sun, and it is looking for you.\n\nThe grey stranger is standing on the beach, watching.
One last fight.
Let it burn.
[From.GetTitledName] went out alone against the dragon of the isle, and killed it, and died of it. The skalds have already made a song of it, and the song has your name in it as the heir of a hero.
Sing it again.
Marooned
This lord is cut off from the world on a small island, presumed drowned by everyone at home.
The Spirit's Blessing
This character freed an air spirit from a split pine, and the wind still keeps them company.
The Mother in the Mere
The mother of the thing that haunted the hall still lives at the bottom of her mere, and some nights she comes up.
The Rebuilt Hall
The island's old hall stands again, cleaned of the thing that haunted it, and the islanders gather in it.
Tribute Ships
Every season a ship comes from the old lands with tribute for the Lord of the Isle.
Death Conceded
This character beat Death at chess. He will come back, but not soon.
Death's Due
This character lost a game of chess to Death, and he took the years they were saving.
Burned by the Dragon
A dragon woke under this island and burned it to the rock.
The Ballad of the Drowned Lord
Skalds and minstrels sing of this character's forebear, who came back from the sea and died fighting a dragon.
Lord of the Isle
This lord was wrecked and given up for drowned, survived on an island, and chose to stay as its free lord.
